title: The Author President
subtitle: Roosevelt in Print
intro: He published a serious naval history at twenty-three, wrote a four-volume frontier epic between political offices, and finished a biography in a room above a store in Medora. Some thirty-five books, thousands of articles, and an estimated hundred thousand letters. Fifteen questions on Roosevelt with a pen.
heroAlt: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent in a hunting camp
heroCredit: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent in hunting camp. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. Cropped from the album mount.

badge.title: The Author President
badge.shareText: I scored {score}/{total} on the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library's Books and Writings quiz — {tier}. Try it:

questions.prompt: Roughly how many books did Roosevelt write?
questions.explanation: Around thirty-five, across history, natural history, memoir, biography and political essays — alongside thousands of articles and an estimated hundred thousand letters. He wrote quickly, in gaps between other work.
questions.imageAlt: The library at Sagamore Hill, photographed by a family member
questions.credit: Taken by one of the family in the library at Sagamore Hill. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What was Roosevelt's first book, begun while he was still at Harvard?
questions.explanation: The Naval War of 1812, started in his final year at Harvard and published in 1882 when he was twenty-three. It was taken seriously as scholarship — the Navy eventually placed a copy aboard every vessel.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as a college student
questions.credit: "Theo. Roosevelt at college." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Which book did Roosevelt write largely in Dakota, in a room above Joe Ferris's store?
questions.explanation: His biography of the Missouri senator Thomas Hart Benton, written through the spring and summer of 1886 between roundup work. He wrote to Lodge that he had finished all but about thirty pages, and confessed to "dreadful misgivings" about it.
questions.imageAlt: The store of Joe Ferris at Medora, North Dakota
questions.credit: The store of Joe Ferris at Medora, N.D. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which of Roosevelt's works is a four-volume history of the American frontier?
questions.explanation: The Winning of the West, published between 1889 and 1896 while he was a civil service commissioner and police commissioner. It is his most ambitious historical work — and the one whose treatment of Native nations reads worst today.
questions.credit: Taken by one of the family in the library at Sagamore Hill. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which famous artist illustrated Roosevelt's Dakota hunting books?
questions.explanation: Frederic Remington, whose drawings did as much as Roosevelt's prose to sell the books and fix the image of the West in the eastern imagination.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in buckskin with a rifle, 1885
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in 1885. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: In July 1899 Governor Roosevelt let it be known that he was taking a whole month's rest. How did he spend it?
options: Writing a biography of Oliver Cromwell
Prospecting a ranch site in Wyoming
Writing the last volume of The Winning of the West
Reading through Gibbon's Decline and Fall
questions.explanation: “I really mean to rest one whole month,” he told his sister Corinne — and then finished the sentence: he did not mean to do one single thing in it, “except write a life of Oliver Cromwell.” She thought that a curious notion of a rest, and said so in the memoir she wrote of him afterwards. He worked at the book through the summer of 1899, in the middle of his term as governor of New York, and Scribner's published it the next year — his third biography, after Thomas Hart Benton and Gouverneur Morris.
questions.imageAlt: A panelled study with bookcases, two desks, leather chairs and framed pictures on the walls
questions.credit: The Governor's office in the New York State Executive Mansion during Roosevelt's term. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's account of his own regiment was published in 1899. What did a satirist suggest it should have been called?
questions.explanation: Finley Peter Dunne, writing as Mr Dooley, suggested "Alone in Cuba" would have been the honest title. Roosevelt wrote to tell him he had enjoyed it — which says something about both men.
questions.imageAlt: Painting of the charge of the Rough Riders
questions.credit: Charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill, reproduction of a painting. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: In 1912 the professional historians of the United States paid Roosevelt a compliment. What did they do?
options: They elected him president of the American Historical Association
They named their prize for narrative history after him
They asked him to write the association's official history
They gave The Winning of the West a lifetime award
questions.explanation: They elected him their president, and on 27 December 1912 he gave the presidential address at their meeting in Boston — seven weeks after losing the election as the Progressive candidate. He called it “History as Literature,” and his argument was that a great historian has to be a writer as well as a researcher: able “to put flesh and blood on dry bones,” to make “dead men living before our eyes.” It is the best short statement of why he wrote the way he did.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt seated in the back of an open touring car, an aide in a bowler hat in front of him
questions.credit: Ex-President Roosevelt in the campaign of 1912. One frame of a Keystone stereograph. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Besides the books, Roosevelt was a relentless letter writer. Roughly how many letters is he estimated to have written?
options: About a hundred and fifty thousand
About three hundred and fifty thousand
questions.explanation: The figure usually given is 150,000, and it began as Roosevelt's own late-life estimate before biographers adopted it — so treat it as an estimate rather than a count. He wrote or dictated to family, cabinet officers, naturalists, children and complete strangers, some letters running to many pages. Elting Morison's edition gathers a fraction of them into eight thick volumes. The earliest to survive was written when he was nine, to his mother.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, three-quarter length portrait, seated. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: When did Roosevelt publish his Autobiography?
questions.explanation: 1913, four years after leaving the presidency and shortly before the Brazilian expedition. It is vivid, selective and occasionally unreliable — he calls the boat thieves "cattle-thieves," for instance — which is why historians read it alongside other sources rather than instead of them.
questions.credit: Taken by one of the family in the library at Sagamore Hill. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which of Roosevelt's books came out of the 1909 expedition?
questions.explanation: African Game Trails. Through the Brazilian Wilderness came out of the later South American expedition — two separate books from two separate journeys, and both written at speed.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and the safari party with a lion
questions.credit: Round the lion. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What kind of writing did Roosevelt send his younger children while travelling?
options: Letters illustrated with his own sketches
questions.explanation: Letters full of pen-and-ink drawings — animals, boats, jokes about the people he was meeting. Published after his death as Theodore Roosevelt's Letters to His Children, they did more for his popular reputation than most of his political work.
questions.imageAlt: Ted, Archie and Ethel Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Ted, Archie, and Ethel Roosevelt one windy day at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's term for journalists who exposed corruption came from which book?
questions.explanation: Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, and its man with the muck-rake who could look no way but downward. Roosevelt meant it as a warning about relentless exposure without hope; the journalists took it as a compliment and kept it.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in his private office
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, 26th President of the United States, in his private office. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt do professionally after leaving the presidency, besides exploring?
options: Ran a New York publishing house
questions.explanation: He wrote for The Outlook as a contributing editor, and later for Metropolitan magazine — using the platform to argue politics and review books. He was, in effect, a working journalist between campaigns: a national readership, a standing column and a deadline, at a time when no other former president had anything of the kind.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, three-quarter length portrait, seated. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Why do historians treat Roosevelt's own accounts with care?
options: He wrote from memory and shaped the story
Most of his manuscripts were destroyed
He wrote much of it in shorthand code
questions.explanation: He wrote fast, from memory, and with an eye to how the story read. The Autobiography gets details wrong, and it is silent about a great deal he did not care to revisit. It is indispensable for his voice and unreliable for dates — which is why any claim worth making gets checked against a second source, and why this Library keeps a corpus to check them against.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent
questions.credit: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent in hunting camp. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. Cropped from the album mount.
